source.title: A universal compression theory for lottery ticket hypothesis and neural scaling laws
source.authors: Hong-Yi Wang; D. Luo; T. Poggio; Isaac L. Chuang; Zi-Yin Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figure labels are imperfectly rendered in the extracted text, but the relevant scaling results are described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper refines the usual scaling-law picture by arguing and demonstrating in synthetic supervised tasks that moment-matching compression can improve the observed scaling exponent. Its experiments are not language-model pretraining scaling studies.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the two Fig.  5 loss-versus-resource scaling comparisons. The paper's cited scaling-law results are not its own findings. Compression-error curves for a generic symmetric function (Fig. 2), training trajectories without a resource-size sweep (Figs. 3–4), and the single transformer-head compression comparison (Fig. 7) do not report scaling-law outcomes for the versions catalogued here.
record.test_reason: The paper starts from the power-law scaling form (citing Kaplan et al.). Its only scaling experiments (Fig. 5) measure how much its own moment-matching compression improves the exponent. They are toy 2D synthetic regression tasks with two-layer nets and MSE loss. No language-model pretraining loss, compute allocation, architecture shape, other-modality pretraining or downstream result is measured. The theoretical claim that power laws can be 'boosted' concerns a compressed-resource axis. It does not dispute that ordinary training follows a power law, so it does not challenge any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but it omits the paper's main, theoretical claims. The authors prove that any smooth permutation-symmetric function of d objects can be compressed to polylog(d) weighted objects with vanishing error, and that this rate is optimal. They use this to prove a 'dynamical lottery ticket hypothesis' and argue power-law scaling in data or width can in principle be boosted to stretched-exponential decay. Fig. 5 is a proof of concept of this, and the algorithm is currently slow and memory-intensive in high dimensions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses moment-matching compression and synthetic supervised MSE experiments, rather than measuring held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy across model, token and compute scales.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different scaling experiments for dataset size and network width, using moment-matching order k=6. It does not report sensitivity of the fitted scaling result to alternative fitting methods.

fits_no_version.finding: In two synthetic 2D regression tasks with two-layer ReLU nets trained by AdamW, test MSE is fitted as a power law in dataset size and in width. Compressing d objects to [16√d] with order-6 moment matching roughly doubles the fitted exponent (Fig. 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Moment-matching compression of data or neurons can raise the effective scaling exponent with respect to the compressed resource in small synthetic regression tasks.

record.problems: The scaling experiments are synthetic supervised regression tasks with MSE, not language-model pretraining. Fig. 5’s exact exponent values are only plotted and are not legible in the extracted text. The paper describes the practical compression algorithm as slow and memory-intensive.
record.rows_left_out: No additional direct scaling-law results omitted. Figures 2–4 and 7 are excluded because they show compression error, training trajectories, or a single compression comparison rather than loss scaling across resource sizes.

untested.parts: All of it: no language-model pretraining loss is measured.
All of it: no extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
All of it: no compute-optimal parameter/token split.
All of it: no depth/width-at-fixed-parameter comparison.
Image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes. Only toy synthetic 2D regression is run, and only to show a compression method's effect.
All of it: no downstream tasks.
All of it: no comparison of fitting choices or curve bending.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled V5 'supports', but the rows measure the study's own compression method in toy regression. The baseline power-law fits are incidental and not in a modality or regime V5 names. The 'doubling' of the exponent is largely built in by choosing d′∝√d. Code is released, and the paper is listed as ICLR 2026.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy for language models, and power-law loss scaling in parameters, tokens or compute with the other resources not bottlenecking.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its trend with compute.
The effect of depth, width and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning and transfer. The reported experiments use synthetic supervised regression tasks and MSE, not language-model pretraining.
Downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Whether fitting choices or other setup changes explain published exponent disagreements, or whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: teacher–student task (two-layer MLP)
rows.size_stated: Dataset size d and compressed size d′; sizes are shown in Fig. 5(a).
rows.operation_detail: Compared test MSE scaling with original versus moment-matching-compressed training datasets; fitted power-law exponents.

conditions.value: d′ rendered in the text as [16√d]; moment-matching order k=6

rows.measure: Test MSE versus dataset size; fitted power-law exponent
rows.value: figure only (compressed dataset-size scaling); authors state compression effectively doubles the scaling exponent
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation error bars; each point averages 10 random instances
rows.note: The text says the exponent α is obtained by fitting L ∝ d−α or d′−α, and reports an effective doubling after compression. The exact plotted exponent values are not recoverable from the extracted figure.
rows.check: The row compares the study's own compression method against the uncompressed baseline, so it is method performance, not a test of V5. The system is a toy teacher–student 2D regression MLP, not a modality or training regime V5 names. The exponent 'doubling' follows almost directly from setting d′=[16√d] when compression is near-lossless. Exponent values are figure-only.
